Section 1: Callaghan Brain and Body Lab Manual 1.1 Welcome Welcome to the Brain and Body Lab at UNSW Sydney! We are so glad that you are joining us, in whatever capacity it is (undergraduate, research assistant, HDR candidate, postdoc, visiting scholar, or collaborator). Academia can be a confusing place, and no two labs are the same. We have written this manual to make your transition into the BABLab as smooth as possible, to share the goals of the lab, its inner workings, as well as its unique culture, to which you will contribute. We hope that during your time here, you will learn a lot about the brain and its interactions with the rest of the body, about developmental psychology, and about science in general. It is our collective goal to have everyone leave the lab with more than they started with, whether that’s new skills, a fresh perspective on a given topic, or a network of colleagues and friends. We hope that you make it your goal to place your own positive stamp on the lab, and to contribute to it in a meaningful way. Just like us, a lab grows and develops over time, and each individual shapes its path. We look forward to seeing what your time in the lab will bring. This manual was originally written at UCLA, and has been revised for the lab’s new home at UNSW Sydney in 2026. It was inspired by several others when first created, and borrows heavily from them (e.g., this one by the Aly Lab and this one from the Ritchey Lab were the primary sources and the main templates used, along with a few others). A lot of time has gone into this document — thinking about what we want our lab to be, what we want to be known for, and how we can make the lab work for everyone. We really respect the principles and ideas we’re aspiring to here, and for that reason, we ask that all new lab members read the manual in full. This lab manual is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution – NonCommercial 4.0 International License. If you want to make your own manual for a lab, or any other purpose, please feel free to take any ideas and inspiration from this one (and cite us), as well as from the others we used when making this (and cite them). 1.2 Mission Statement In the BABLab we aim to do good science that makes a difference. That is our mission. To do it, we need people to be passionate about what we are doing and come to work in a good frame of mind to get it done. We aim to be nurturing, challenging, and stimulating to students. We aim to be respectful, engaging, and meaningful for families and participants. 1.3 Diversity Commitment We in the BABLab value the diversity of our lab members and research participants. We are committed to learning, understanding, and dismantling systems of oppression, particularly in academia, and to being genuine allies to First Nations peoples and other historically marginalised communities. You are welcome in this lab whatever the colour of your skin, your sexual orientation, your gender identity, your nationality, your ability, and your culture. We acknowledge the Bedegal (Bidjigal) people as the Traditional Custodians of the land on which UNSW’s Kensington campus stands, and pay our respects to Elders past and present. Sovereignty over this land was never ceded. Supporting Indigenous participation in research and academia. We are committed to engaging with UNSW’s Nura Gili Centre for Indigenous Programs to identify pathways for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students to take part in the lab’s research (e.g., through Indigenous Honours or HDR pathways coordinated with Nura Gili), and to consulting Nura Gili early whenever a study’s design, recruitment, or data involves Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander participants or communities. Any such research will be conducted in line with the AIATSIS Code of Ethics for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Research and the NHMRC’s Ethical Guidelines for Research with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.

Section 2: Expectations and Responsibilities 2.1 Everyone Big Picture Sometimes science can be hard, and the rewards (interesting research findings, papers, etc.) can be few and far between. However, science is always fun when we make the lab a great place to be. In the BABLab, we want everyone to have a positive experience that is free from hostility, so that people can do their best, most productive science. Great labs don’t just happen, they are built. Here is what we can all do to help: Do work that you are proud of. Work carefully, and strategically. Do not rush. Respect our participants. Whether they are families, undergrads, or adults from the community, they are giving up their time to be involved in research. Always act professionally with participants over the phone and in person, and do not leave them waiting. Keep in mind that participants may have different political and religious beliefs, sexual orientations, family compositions, and life experiences to you and/or your friends and family. Please conduct yourself in a way that respects their unique situation and personhood. Respect our child participants. In addition to the above point, remember that children are to be respected as much as adults. Please be aware that even well-meaning adults can sound patronising sometimes when speaking with children. At the risk of sounding patronising myself, comments like “cool shoes” are fine, but comments like “you are so cute” are not in this context. Respect the data and the people who collected it. Data collection, especially in developmental populations, is hard. People put real effort into it — coming in on weekends, after hours, on holidays. You might be analysing data that you did not have to collect. That is a pretty great situation, so make sure you treat that data in the same way you would your own. Respect your lab mates: their culture, religion, beliefs, sexual orientation, and personality quirks. Science is for everyone. Respect yourself: your need for time off, your happiness, your other commitments. You are responsible for constructing your own boundaries. Be supportive of your lab mates. We are a team. Science is about collaboration, not competition. Be forgiving of yourself and one another. Academic environments can be challenging. We all make mistakes, and not everyone is on their A-game every day. Whatever happens, try to be understanding, forgive, and move on. Tension or hostility in the lab affects everyone, and behaving in a bullying, intimidating, rude, or disrespectful way will not be tolerated. I expect everyone to be mature and professional while in the lab — this is a workplace and should be treated as one. If there are any problems which cannot be dealt with in the lab, please tell Bridget. If the concern involves Bridget herself, or you’d simply rather not raise it with her directly, you can instead contact `[UNSW Complaints (https://www.unsw.edu.au/complaints), or use UNSW’s confidential Complaints Management and Investigation channels. Be honest with yourself and others. This means that if you notice a mistake, however embarrassing, admit it, correct it, and move on. Check everything several times. Then get someone else to check it. Then check it again. It’s ok to make mistakes, but mistakes shouldn’t be because of carelessness or rushed work. Under no circumstances is it ok to plagiarise, tamper with data, make up data, or omit data. If you are feeling pressured to succeed and think that is interfering with your judgement, reach out to Bridget so you can talk about it. Pressure is something we all face and is not an excuse to engage in research misconduct (see Section 3). If you are struggling with health and/or unhappiness, or you see someone else struggling, please come and see me (Bridget). Everyone goes through rough patches, and we want to help each other out. UNSW also has free, confidential support: the Psychology & Wellness Service for students, and the Employee Assistance Program (via Converge International) for staff and their immediate family, which is free and available any time. Have a life outside of the lab, take care of your mental and physical health, and don’t ever feel bad for taking time off work — and don’t make others feel bad for doing that either. Small Picture There are a few day-to-day things to keep in mind to keep the lab running smoothly. Remote and hybrid work When we’re not all in the same room, it’s even more important to check Teams chat and email regularly and be available to respond to messages, and to set up virtual meetings when needed. Keep participant-facing conduct professional in virtual meetings the same way you would in person — appropriate background, and appropriate dress if participants might see you. General If you’re sick, please take time off, stay home, and take care of yourself. Just message the lab manager or me (Bridget) to let us know. If you know you might be unwell (e.g., you have minor surgery scheduled and don’t know how well you’ll recover), play it safe and reschedule your appointments ahead of time. Working in developmental populations means work times need to be flexible. If you are collecting data or recruiting participants, you may be expected to work some weekends and holidays. We will share that burden as evenly as possible, and where this applies to paid staff, hours will be tracked and managed in line with your employment conditions (see Hours below) — talk to Bridget or the lab manager about time-in-lieu arrangements before, not after, taking on extra hours. Outside of data collection and recruitment, you are not expected to work or come into the lab on weekends or holidays, and you are not expected to stay late at night. You are expected to get your work done to a high standard, in whatever time of day best suits your work style. That said, being in lab some of the time is important for the lab and for morale, so you shouldn’t work remotely all of the time. All HDR candidates, postdocs, research assistants, and paid employees (e.g., lab managers) are expected to attend lab meetings when their schedules allow. We will set a time for lab meeting each term that best fits everyone’s schedule. Volunteers and other students are expected to attend lab meeting when it suits their schedule and interest. Make sure the lab is locked if no one is inside, turn off the lights if you’re the last one leaving, and water the plants if they’re looking sad. Keep the lab tidy. Eating in lab is fine, but clean up food waste, crumbs, and spills. Put lab equipment back where you found it. Keep common areas uncluttered. Lab is a shared space. Unless you have been assigned a permanent desk, do not permanently claim a space. Use space when it’s available and remove your belongings when you leave so others can use it. Dress code is casual, neat, and approachable. When interacting with participants or presenting your work, don’t wear pyjamas, dirty clothes, clothes with holes in them, or clothes that are see-through. Jeans are fine, and even active wear is fine when you’re collecting data (you might end up on the floor with a toddler). If you want to dress up, that’s fine too — as long as you’re comfortable and approachable. When you are running participants, show up 15–20 minutes early to set everything up. Be on time for your meetings: respect that others have busy schedules and everyone’s time is valuable. If you need to cancel a meeting, please do so as early as possible so that other meetings/activities can be arranged in its place 2.2 Principal Investigator All of the above, and I will… Support your scientific development and be responsive to your emotional needs. Give you feedback on a timely basis, including on project ideas, conference posters, talks, manuscripts, figures, and grants. Write and submit scientific papers (including review papers) in a timely manner. Help train and mentor students in the lab (both undergraduate and HDR). Seek out opportunities to present your work (e.g., at departmental events, in other labs, at conferences). Please see Bridget early about identifying grant mechanisms to target and for example applications. Apply for jobs (academic or otherwise) when you’re ready, after discussing your progress with Bridget. Postdoctoral training can lead to many different jobs — academia, industry, and elsewhere. This includes knowing the literature like the back of your hand. Take ownership of your project. Create, submit, respond to, and monitor adherence to UNSW ethics for your research projects Create publicly accessible Wiki’s (hosted on Github) for each of your research projects (see Bridget for examples) Create Standard Operating Procedures for every component of your study, link them to the Wiki, and make them publicly available (on Github) Learn to code in R, and establish data cleaning and analysis scripts in R, that you comprehensively annotate and store in Github (linking them to published manuscripts where appropriate) Curate your datasets for public use at the completion of your research project, and where allowed, store them on Github. Meet UNSW’s Research Progress Review milestones, starting with Confirmation of Candidature within your first 9–12 months (for PhD candidates), and subsequent Progress Reviews at the intervals your program requires. Think critically about what you want for your career (academia — research or teaching, industry, science communication, something else). Section 3: Code of Conduct 3.1 Essential Policies 3.2 Scientific Integrity 3.3 Human Subjects Research

Section 3: Code of Conduct 3.1 Essential Policies UNSW Code of Conduct and Values UNSW has a Code of Conduct and Values, which applies to staff and students across all teaching, learning, and research activities, and a separate Student Code of Conduct process for handling breaches. Please take the time to familiarise yourself with both before you start in the lab. 3.2 Scientific Integrity Reproducible Research The BABLab is committed to performing reproducible research. Reproducible research means that if you gave someone your raw data and analysis code, they should be able to reproduce your results exactly. If they can’t, it suggests that something is wrong (e.g., a mistake in the pipeline) or that you didn’t properly document the data collection, cleaning, or analysis process. Neither of these is good. Therefore, we take steps to make sure all aspects of data collection, cleaning, and analysis are extremely well documented. For results to be reproducible, you need to be organised and document everything! Take detailed notes on your study design, save all citations for questionnaires you use, and if you make up a questionnaire yourself, document that it was custom-made for the study, so that no one spends hours down the track looking for a citation that doesn’t exist. Keep notes on recruitment methods, inclusion/exclusion criteria, participant scheduling, all research protocols, and any changes to protocols that occur during the study. If something goes wrong or something unusual happens, document that too. Document scanner/equipment parameters and the software versions used to collect data. Before you start collecting data, build a wiki page that documents every component of the study and update it as a living document throughout. This wiki should contain everything anyone would ever need to know about your study. Once you’ve collected data, take detailed notes on data cleaning and analysis. Even if you’ve preregistered your study design (which you very likely will), you still need to document this stage, as you may move away from your preregistered choices for a variety of reasons — you need to know and record what those reasons are. Write down how you did things, in what order, from pre-processing through to statistical tests. Your code should also be clearly commented, so it’s understandable months later by you or by an outsider. It is highly encouraged that you use version control (e.g., Git with GitHub) to track code changes and share code with others. In sum: write copious notes on your study design and measures before you start, and put all of it in the wiki. Write beautifully annotated analysis code (e.g., in R Markdown or Quarto) and put it on GitHub. There is nothing more satisfying in science (or life) than a well-organised study. Authorship Like other labs, we follow the APA guidelines with respect to authorship: “Authorship credit should reflect the individual’s contribution to the study. An author is considered anyone involved with initial research design, data collection and analysis, manuscript drafting, and final approval. However, the following do not necessarily qualify for authorship: providing funding or resources, mentorship, or contributing research but not helping with the publication itself. The primary author assumes responsibility for the publication, making sure that the data are accurate, that all deserving authors have been credited, that all authors have given their approval to the final draft, and handles responses to inquiries after the manuscript is published.” This aligns with UNSW’s Research Authorship, Publication and Dissemination Policy, which lab members should also read. We use the CRediT authorship taxonomy to record specific contributions. Issues with authorship should be raised with Bridget — and to head off disputes before they start, any new project should agree an authorship order (or at least the principles for deciding one) in writing at the outset, revisited if the project’s shape changes substantially. Old Projects If an HDR candidate or postdoc drives a project and/or collects a dataset but does not analyse it, write it up, or actively work on it within a reasonable time frame after data collection ends, Bridget may discuss handing the project off to someone who can complete it, to expedite publication. If someone no longer wishes to work on a project, or no longer wants to be an author, Bridget will reassign the project. This policy exists to prevent data — especially expensive data, e.g., fMRI — from remaining unpublished. Remember the lab philosophy: “do good science that makes a difference.” We can’t make a difference if research isn’t disseminated. Responsible Conduct of Research All research in the BABLab is conducted under the Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research, the national framework covering honesty, rigour, transparency, fairness, and accountability in research. All HDR candidates must complete UNSW’s Responsible Conduct of Research (RCR) training, and Bridget, as supervisor, is responsible for guiding, mentoring, and monitoring that training. Everyone in the lab — not just HDR candidates — should read and understand the Code. If you have a concern about a possible breach of the Code (by anyone, at any level), you can raise it with Bridget, or speak confidentially with one of UNSW’s Research Integrity Advisors, who exist specifically to advise on this without it needing to go through your supervisor first. 3.3 Human Subjects Research Adherence to approved human research ethics approvals is essential, and non-adherence can lead to severe consequences for the entire lab (i.e., we may lose permission to run any research on human participants). Part of respecting our participants means we must strictly adhere to the approved protocol for each project. All lab members must read the ethics approval documents and consent forms for any project they’re working on. This is also a great way to familiarise yourself with a project, and you’re welcome to read the approvals for other lab projects you’re not working on, to learn more about them. If you’re not named on a project’s ethics approval (e.g., a volunteer with the lab), you cannot run participants, look at the data, analyse the data, or be involved with the project in any way. At UNSW, human research ethics approval is granted by a Human Research Ethics Advisory Panel (HREAP) — there are several discipline-based panels, and the relevant one is determined by the Coordinating Chief Investigator’s School or Faculty. Applications are submitted as a Human Research Ethics Application (HREA). Lab members must complete the human research ethics training specified for the protocols they’re listed on. Speak to your lab manager about which protocols you’ll be listed on and what training is required, plus how to access and document it. If you’re starting your own project, you’ll be expected to write your own HREA (see Bridget and your lab manager for help). If you’re starting a study within an existing project, you’ll need to write an amendment to that project’s approval. If you’re joining an existing project, you’ll need to be added to that project’s approved personnel list (see your HDR, postdoc, or lab manager mentor about this). You must have ethics approval before collecting, looking at, or using any human participant data. Part of human research ethics training covers reporting of incidental or unexpected events. If a participant falls ill, becomes very upset, has an accident with lab equipment, is injured, or is otherwise adversely affected by participating in a study, tell Bridget so we can report this to the relevant HREAP and/or funding agencies as required. If your research involves Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander participants, communities, or data, additional obligations apply under the AIATSIS Code of Ethics and NHMRC guidelines — see Section 1.3 and talk to Bridget and Nura Gili before designing the study, not after ethics submission.

Section 4: Use of AI in the Lab

Section 4: Use of AI in the Lab Generative AI tools (large language models, coding assistants, transcription/translation tools, etc.) are now a normal part of research work, and we want lab members to use them well rather than either avoiding them out of caution or leaning on them uncritically. The guiding principle: AI can help you work, but it cannot do your thinking for you, and it never reduces your responsibility for what you submit. What’s generally fine Using AI to search literature, summarise papers, or get oriented in an unfamiliar area — as a starting point, not a substitute for reading the primary sources yourself. Using AI coding assistants to write, debug, or explain code, provided you understand every line well enough to explain it to someone else and have verified the output does what you think it does (see Section 3 on reproducible research — “I don’t know why it works” is not an acceptable answer for analysis code). Using AI for grammar, clarity, or copyediting on drafts you wrote. Using AI to help draft routine, non-sensitive material — e.g., a first pass at a recruitment flyer, an email template, a slide outline. Using AI to help with formatting, restructuring, or generating boilerplate (references in a particular style, a data dictionary skeleton, regex, etc.). What’s not fine Using AI to generate, fabricate, or “clean up” data or results. This is research misconduct — see Section 3 — regardless of whether AI was involved. Pasting unpublished data, participant-identifiable information, consent forms, or draft manuscripts under review into a consumer AI tool that isn’t covered by a UNSW data protection agreement (see Confidentiality below). Letting an AI tool write substantive sections of a paper, grant, or thesis without disclosure and without you having fully verified the content and claims. You are responsible for every citation, number, and claim in anything with your name on it — AI tools regularly invent plausible-sounding references and mis-state findings, and “the AI made it up” is not a defence. Listing an AI tool as an author. It cannot take responsibility for the work, cannot give consent to being listed, and does not meet any authorship standard we use (APA, CRediT, or UNSW’s own policy — see Section 3). Using AI-generated text or analysis in place of your own understanding when you’re being assessed on that understanding (e.g., HDR milestones, coursework). Confidentiality and data protection This is the part that matters most given we work with children’s and families’ data. UNSW has activated Microsoft Copilot with Commercial Data Protection for everyone with a zID — this is currently the only generative AI tool that’s appropriate for anything involving UNSW research data, because inputs aren’t used to train external models and are covered by UNSW’s data agreements. Consumer tools (a personal ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini account, browser extensions, random “AI note-taker” apps) are not appropriate for anything containing participant data, even de-identified data, unless you’ve specifically checked with Bridget and the lab manager first. When in doubt, treat it like you would any other cloud service you haven’t vetted — don’t put lab data into it. Disclosure If you use AI tools in a way that materially shaped a piece of work (drafting, analysis, figure generation), disclose it — in the manuscript’s methods/acknowledgements per the target journal’s policy, in your thesis per UNSW’s requirements, and to Bridget before it goes out the door. This isn’t about penalising AI use; it’s the same transparency logic as the rest of Section 3 — if someone needs to know how a result was produced in order to evaluate or reproduce it, tell them. If you’re ever unsure whether a particular use is fine, ask Bridget or your mentor before proceeding rather than after — this is a fast-moving area and the answer may be “let’s think about this one.”

Section 5: Data Access and Management

Section 5: Data Access and Management Where lab data lives Day-to-day project files (protocols, in-progress analysis, wiki drafts, non-final data) live on UNSW OneDrive/SharePoint (Microsoft 365), which is approved for research data from Public up to Highly Sensitive classifications — provided multi-factor authentication is enabled, which it should be by default on your UNSW account. Everything stored there stays on servers physically located in Australia and is retained for a minimum of seven years, with a 60-day recovery window if something is accidentally deleted. Classify data honestly when you create it: Public — things like published papers, de-identified aggregate summaries. Private — most day-to-day working files. Sensitive — identifiable participant data, unpublished results. Highly Sensitive — anything where a breach could cause real harm (e.g., identifiable data on minors, health information, anything a participant would reasonably expect strong protection for). Sensitive and Highly Sensitive data may need additional encryption or access restrictions beyond the OneDrive/SharePoint default — check with RDM@unsw.edu.au (UNSW’s research data management team) if you’re not sure what’s required for your project, and ask before you start collecting, not after. Access permissions Not everyone needs access to everything. As a rule: raw, identifiable data is restricted to people named on the relevant ethics approval for that project (see Section 3); de-identified/cleaned datasets can be shared more widely within the lab once they exist. When the lab manager sets up a new project’s folder structure, permissions should be set at that point, not left open by default. If you’re leaving the lab or rolling off a project, your access should be reviewed and removed if it’s no longer needed. Long-term archiving and sharing For data the lab is finished actively working with: Smaller behavioural/questionnaire datasets: the Open Science Framework remains a good option, alongside UNSW’s own Research Data Archive for long-term institutional preservation. Neuroimaging data: OpenNeuro. Microbiome data: the Sequence Read Archive or European Nucleotide Archive. Studies with specific funder data-sharing mandates (e.g., NIH-funded studies inherited from UCLA, or any future NHMRC/ARC-funded work) will have their own requirements — check with Bridget before sharing anything from those studies specifically. As before: share code and data freely within the lab (aligning with ethics requirements), but don’t share anything with the outside world until the lab has finished working with it and Bridget has agreed it’s ready. Retention Under the Australian Code for the Responsible Conduct of Research, research data and primary materials must generally be retained for a minimum of 5 years from publication (longer for clinical or otherwise higher-risk research — check the specific requirement for your project type). In practice, UNSW’s default 7-year retention on OneDrive/SharePoint covers this, but retention obligations survive even if someone leaves the lab, so departing lab members cannot take the only copy of anything with them. Moving data across institutions and borders If you’re bringing a dataset with you from a previous institution (e.g., UCLA), or collaborating with researchers overseas, that’s a genuine cross-border data transfer, not just a file copy. It needs a data-sharing/data-transfer agreement between the institutions (talk to Bridget and UNSW Research Services before moving anything with identifiable participant information), and it needs to be covered by the relevant HREAP approval at UNSW as well as whatever approval covered the original collection. Devices and everyday security Use UNSW-managed or UNSW-approved devices and accounts for anything involving participant data — not personal laptops, personal cloud storage, or personal email. Use a password manager and unique passwords; enable MFA everywhere it’s offered. Never leave identifiable data (paper or digital) unattended in testing rooms or common areas. If you lose a device, or suspect any account or data has been compromised, tell Bridget and the lab manager immediately — this may need to be reported to UNSW IT and, depending on what’s involved, to the relevant HREAP. Approved tools Data collection tools (e.g., Qualtrics, REDCap) and any new software should be checked against UNSW’s approved-vendor and data-storage-location requirements before adoption. Ask the lab manager or RDM@unsw.edu.au before locking in a new tool for a study.

Section 6: Data Analysis & Code Practices

Section 6: Data Analysis & Code Practices Every analysis project in the lab — from an undergraduate’s first script to the code behind a submitted paper — gets a GitHub repository, and every repository is expected to meet the same baseline. One repo per project Each study or sub-project gets its own repository under the lab’s GitHub organisation, named clearly (e.g. mindbrainbody-interoception-followup, not analysis2 or finalfinal). Don’t bury a project’s code inside someone’s personal miscellaneous repo — if you leave the lab, the project’s code needs to be findable without you. What goes on GitHub, and what never does Code goes on GitHub. Raw or identifiable participant data never does — not even in a private repo. GitHub is not an approved storage location for participant data under UNSW’s data classification rules (see Data Access & Management); a repo being private doesn’t change that. In practice: Scripts should read data from its actual location on OneDrive/SharePoint (or wherever the project’s approved storage lives), referenced by a relative path, not a hardcoded path to a specific person’s laptop. Add a .gitignore that explicitly excludes data folders, so a stray git add . can’t accidentally commit a CSV full of participant responses. The lab manager can provide a standard .gitignore template — use it as your starting point for every new repo. If a repo genuinely needs example data to run (e.g., so someone else can test the pipeline), use a small simulated or fully de-identified synthetic dataset built for that purpose, clearly labelled as such. If you’re ever unsure whether something is safe to commit, ask before pushing, not after. Script and repo structure Every repo has a README.md explaining, in plain language: what the project is, what each script does and the order to run them in, what the expected inputs and outputs are, and who to contact with questions. Link back to the study’s wiki page rather than duplicating everything. Every script starts with a short header comment: what it does, who wrote it, when, and what it expects as input. Follow the tidyverse style guide for formatting (the styler package will do most of this for you automatically) — consistency matters more than anyone’s personal preference, because someone else will read this code. Use relative paths (e.g., via the here package) rather than absolute paths like C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/. A script that only runs on the machine that wrote it is not reproducible. Prefer R Markdown or Quarto documents over bare .R scripts for anything that produces reported results — narrative, code, and output living in one place makes it far easier for someone (including future-you) to follow what happened and why. Reproducibility mechanics Set a seed explicitly (set.seed()) anywhere randomness is involved (bootstrapping, permutation tests, train/test splits), and note why that seed and not another, if it matters. Record the analysis environment: run sessioninfo::session_info() at the end of your analysis and save the output alongside your results, so package versions are documented. For larger or long-running projects, use renv to lock package versions for the whole project. Scripts should regenerate figures and tables from raw data through to the final output. If a figure in a paper was hand-edited after being exported from R, that’s a red flag — the pipeline should produce the reportable output directly, or the manual edit should be documented and justified. Version control workflow Commit early, commit often, and write commit messages that explain why, not just what (“switch to robust SEs after reviewer comment” beats “update analysis.R”). Use branches for exploratory or risky changes rather than working directly on main. Before merging any script that produces results going into a manuscript, thesis chapter, or conference presentation into main, have another lab member review it — run it themselves if possible, not just read it. This is the same “check it, then get someone else to check it” principle from Section 2, applied to code. When a manuscript is submitted, tag the exact commit that produced the reported results (e.g., v1.0-submission) so the analysis that generated a specific set of numbers stays addressable even as the code keeps evolving afterward. This also sets you up to mint a Zenodo DOI for the code release alongside the paper, consistent with the lab’s open science policy (Section 5.8). Defaults on visibility New analysis repos are private by default while a project is active (see Section 5.8, Open Science) and made public — ideally alongside a tagged, citable release — once Bridget agrees the lab is done working with it and it accompanies a preprint or publication. Don’t make a repo public “to be safe” before that point.

Section 7: Training Resources MRI / fMRI Analysis Microbiome Bioinformatics (QIIME 2) R (general, and for stats/reproducible analysis)

Section 7: Training Resources MRI / fMRI Analysis Andy’s Brain Book — the best starting point for anyone new to fMRI analysis. Free, self-paced, and walks through a full analysis from raw data to results using FSL, AFNI, or SPM (pick whichever your project uses - we use FSL typically). Also has dedicated tutorials on BIDS and fMRIPrep (see below). FSL Course materials (Oxford FMRIB/WIN) — the in-person course has a fee, but Oxford posts the full lecture recordings, slides, and practicals from past courses online for free, including an “Introduction to Neuroimaging Analysis” primer that’s a good first read before touching FSL itself. BIDS Starter Kit — the Brain Imaging Data Structure is the standard way to organise raw MRI data now, and most modern pipelines (fMRIPrep, MRIQC) expect it. Worth doing before you collect a single scan on a new study, not after. fMRIPrep tutorials — Andy’s Brain Book’s fMRIPrep walkthrough and the Carpentries Incubator lesson on exploring fMRIPrep outputs are both free and hands-on. Neurohackademy (University of Washington) — a two-week summer institute whose lecture recordings and tutorial materials (Python, reproducibility, Git/GitHub, neuroimaging data science) are posted freely online every year, also indexed on INCF TrainingSpace. The Princeton Handbook for Reproducible Neuroimaging — less a course, more a practical reference for doing neuroimaging analysis reproducibly (directory structure, pipelines, common pitfalls). Microbiome Bioinformatics (QIIME 2) Microbiome Bioinformatics with QIIME 2 — free online workshop — the official QIIME 2 team’s ~12-hour workshop, released free with recorded lectures and hands-on tutorials, covering import/demultiplexing/denoising through diversity analyses. Also on YouTube. QIIME 2 Current Protocols documentation — a more formal, citable end-to-end walkthrough of a complete microbiome analysis, good as a reference once you’ve done the workshop. QIIME 2 Forum — genuinely useful for troubleshooting; the developers and community answer questions directly, and it’s searchable for issues you’ll likely hit early on. R (general, and for stats/reproducible analysis) Learning Statistics with R (Danielle Navarro) — a full, free, open-licence textbook aimed specifically at psychology students learning R and statistics together. Probably the single best starting point for anyone in the lab who is new to both R and stats. R for Data Science (2nd ed.) (Wickham & Grolemund) — free online, the standard reference for the tidyverse approach to importing, cleaning, and visualising data in R. Good next step once you’re comfortable with the basics. Data Carpentry / Software Carpentry R lessons — free, self-paced, workshop-style lessons that assume no prior programming experience; also cover the command line and Git, which pairs well with the reproducibility practices in Section 3. swirl — an R package that teaches R interactively inside the R console itself (install it, run swirl(), and it walks you through exercises with immediate feedback). Good for people who learn better by typing than by reading. Tidyverse Style Guide — the style guide the lab’s code conventions are based on (see Data Analysis & Code Practices). Pair it with the styler package, which will reformat existing code to match automatically. Advanced R (Wickham) — free online, for once you’re past the basics and want to understand how R actually works under the hood (useful once you’re writing your own functions rather than just running analyses). A very basic tutorial for performing linear mixed effects analyses (Bodo Winter, PDF) — the tutorial most people in developmental/cognitive psychology cite as their entry point into lme4 and mixed models; short, practical, and aimed at exactly this kind of repeated-measures/nested data. If you find other free resources that were useful to you, add them to this section — this list should keep growing as tools change.
section-8-essential-reading-list.html

Section 8: Essential Reading List 1. Brain–Gut Axis and Mental Health 2. Adversity and the Microbiome 3. Interoception, Mental Health, and the Theory of Constructed Emotion 4. Pregnancy and Intergenerational Mental Health 5. Perinatal Health 6. Oral Microbiome

Section 8: Essential Reading List Here are some papers (and a couple of books) that have shaped how we think about brain–body development. For new lab members: read what’s relevant to your project first, then work through the rest as you have time. 1. Brain–Gut Axis and Mental Health Citation Notes Sudo, N. et al. (2004). Postnatal microbial colonization programs the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal system for stress response in mice. The Journal of Physiology. An earlier paper in the field that was really influential. It showed that germ-free mice have an elevated ‘stress’ response, and colonizing them with bacteria early in life normalizes many of their different indices — timing of colonization matters, which suggests a sensitive period for the impacts of the microbiome on brain development. Cryan, J.F. & Dinan, T.G. (2012). Mind-altering microorganisms: the impact of the gut microbiota on brain and behavior. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. Still the most-cited overview in the field. The figures are especially nice and I often use them in talks to demonstrate the pathways of brain–gut communication. O’Mahony, S.M. et al. (2009). Early life stress alters behavior, immunity, and microbiota in rats: implications for irritable bowel syndrome and psychiatric illnesses. Biological Psychiatry. Maternal separation alters the microbiome, not just behavior, as well as immunity. This paper was the first time I realized that the same stressors which alter the pace of brain development and increase anxious behaviors in mice are also models for irritable bowel syndrome. Diaz Heijtz, R. et al. (2011). Normal gut microbiota modulates brain development and behavior. PNAS. Companion piece to Sudo. Microbiota shape brain gene expression and behavior, and there’s a window early in development when this matters most. Clarke, G. et al. (2013). The microbiome-gut-brain axis during early life regulates the hippocampal serotonergic system in a sex-dependent manner. Molecular Psychiatry. Early microbiome effects on hippocampal serotonin differ by sex. Bercik, P. et al. (2011). The intestinal microbiota affect central levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor and behavior in mice. Gastroenterology. Transferring microbiota (fecal microbiome transplant – FMT) changes behavior and brain in mice. Tillisch, K. et al. (2013). Consumption of fermented milk product with probiotic modulates brain activity. Gastroenterology. This paper came out right before Bridget started her postdoc at Columbia. It was an exciting proof of concept for the use of neuroimaging and microbiome manipulations together. Cryan, J.F. et al. (2019). The microbiota-gut-brain axis. Physiological Reviews. Huge. Don’t try to read it cover to cover — treat it as a reference for whenever you need a citation for something specific. Vuong, H.E., Yano, J.M., Fung, T.C. & Hsiao, E.Y. (2017). The Microbiome and Host Behavior. Annual Review of Neuroscience. Another solid comprehensive review, this one leans a bit more into social behavior and neurodevelopment and is actually my favorite review paper on the topic. Cowan, C.S.M., Dinan, T.G. & Cryan, J.F. (2020). Annual Research Review: Critical windows – the microbiota-gut-brain axis in neurocognitive development. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. Makes the case that microbiome development and brain development share sensitive periods. Ties a lot of the above together. Valles-Colomer, M. et al. (2019). The neuroactive potential of the human gut microbiota* Nature Microbiology*. This paper describes the brain-gut module - a method for narrowing the space for metagenomic pathways of potential interest for psychologists/psychiatrists Books (there are many, but these two are my favorite) Citation Notes Yong, E. (2016). I Contain Multitudes: The Microbes Within Us and a Grander View of Life. Ecco/HarperCollins. Ed Yong is excellent — I love all his books, and this one I love the best. Great entry into thinking about the wonder of the microbiome. Enders, G. (2015). Gut: The Inside Story of Our Body’s Most Underrated Organ. Greystone Books. Breezier read, mostly digestion and gut anatomy, touches on the brain connection near the end. Good starting point for entering the field. 2. Adversity and the Microbiome Citation Notes Callaghan, B.L., Fields, A., Gee, D.G., Gabard-Durnam, L., Caldera, C., Humphreys, K.L., Goff, B., Flannery, J., Telzer, E.H., Shapiro, M. & Tottenham, N. (2020). Mind and gut: Associations between mood and gastrointestinal distress in children exposed to adversity. Development and Psychopathology. One of the first studies to connect childhood adversity, gut microbiome disruption, and brain activity in kids, using an adoption sample. It is a proof-of-concept study in a small sample — so take it with a grain of salt. But this is basically the paper that kicked off this line of research in the lab. Reid, B.M., Horne, R., Donzella, B., Szamosi, J.C., Coe, C.L., Foster, J.A. & Gunnar, M.R. (2021). Microbiota-immune alterations in adolescents following early life adversity: A proof of concept study. Developmental Psychobiology. Takes the adversity–microbiome story into adolescence, and adds an immune angle. Hantsoo, L., Jašarević, E., Criniti, S., McGeehan, B., Tanes, C., Sammel, M.D., Elovitz, M.A., Compher, C., Wu, G. & Epperson, C.N. (2019). Childhood adversity impact on gut microbiota and inflammatory response to stress during pregnancy. Brain, Behavior, and Immunity. Same idea, but in pregnant women. Childhood adversity is linked to a different gut microbiome composition and a different stress response, years later, during pregnancy. 3. Interoception, Mental Health, and the Theory of Constructed Emotion Citation Notes Craig, A.D. (2002). How do you feel? Interoception: the sense of the physiological condition of the body. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. I have only skimmed these but Paul cites a lot — Paul, what do you think? Atzil, S. et al. (2017). Growing a social brain. Nature Human Behaviour. Excellent paper describing how interoception is built up through our interactions in the social world from the earliest stages of life. This paper challenges traditional views of attachment as being driven by the ‘secure base’. Murphy, J. et al. (2017). Interoception and psychopathology – a developmental neuroscience perspective. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. Great review on how to think about interoception across the lifespan (including pregnancy). Barrett, L.F. et al. (2016). An active inference theory of allostasis and interoception in depression. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B. Great account of the locked-in model of depression. Barrett, L.F. & Simmons, W.K. (2015). Interoceptive predictions in the brain. Nature Reviews Neuroscience. The predictive-coding mechanics behind Barrett’s theory. Seth, A.K. & Friston, K.J. (2016). Active interoceptive inference and the emotional brain. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B. A parallel account from a different lab. Barrett, L.F. (2017). The theory of constructed emotion: an active inference account of interoception and categorization. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience. The Theory of Constructed Emotion. If you are like me you will need to read this multiple times, but it’s worth understanding — it shapes a lot of the ways we are asking questions (or at least trying to) in the lab now. Interoception Summit 2016 participants / Khalsa, S.S. et al. (2018). Interoception and Mental Health: A Roadmap. Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging. This was the offshoot of a conference on interoception and is a great paper for linking interoception and mental health. Garfinkel, S.N., Seth, A.K., Barrett, A.B., Suzuki, K. & Critchley, H.D. (2015). Knowing your own heart: distinguishing interoceptive accuracy from interoceptive awareness. Biological Psychology. Defines accuracy, sensibility, and awareness as separate constructs — this is essential reading for people studying interoception in the lab. Savoca, P.W. et al. (under review). Understanding Interoceptive Modeling and Categorization Following Early-Life Adversity. Defines two distinct constructs of interoception: interoceptive modeling (the process via which the nervous system predicts and tracks sensory information from the periphery to generate a model of the current or future state of the body) and interoceptive categorization (the categorization and interpretation of that information). 4. Pregnancy and Intergenerational Mental Health Citation Notes Barker, D.J.P. (1995). The fetal origins of adult disease. Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The original DOHaD paper. Not about mental health — about birth weight and cardiovascular disease. But this is a really important paper for the field. Entringer, S., Buss, C. & Wadhwa, P.D. (2015). Prenatal stress, development, health and disease risk: a psychobiological perspective. Psychoneuroendocrinology. A good review on prenatal stress and offspring biological outcomes across a range of domains. Yehuda, R. & Lehrner, A. (2018). Intergenerational transmission of trauma effects: putative role of epigenetic mechanisms. World Psychiatry. Yehuda has done a lot of studies on intergenerational transmission: holocaust survivors, combat veterans, the 9/11 cohort, and all of that research is reviewed here. Dias, B.G. & Ressler, K.J. (2014). Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations. Nature Neuroscience. The mouse version of intergenerational transmission. Threat-condition a smell in one generation, and the grandchildren who were never exposed to that smell are reactive to it too. Callaghan, B.L., Cowan, C.S.M. & Richardson, R. (2016). Treating generational stress: Effect of paternal stress on development of memory and extinction in offspring is reversed by probiotic treatment. Psychological Science. Rats exposed to maternal separation as infants show long-lasting memories of cues tied to shock (unusual — they typically forget really quickly). Those male rats, as adults, sire a new generation, and those pups also show the longer-lasting memories of threat-related stimuli, despite not being directly exposed to stressors themselves. Giving the dads or the second-generation pups probiotics gets rid of that intergenerational transmission of threat behavior. Directly ties the microbiome into intergenerational transmission. 5. Perinatal Health Citation Notes Glynn, L.M., Howland, M.A. & Fox, M. (2018). Maternal programming: Application of a developmental psychopathology perspective. Development and Psychopathology. Argues that pregnancy is a sensitive period for the mother’s brain too, not just the baby’s. Reframes a conversation that’s usually all about the fetus. Monk, C., Lugo-Candelas, C. & Trumpff, C. (2019). Prenatal Developmental Origins of Future Psychopathology: Mechanisms and Pathways. Annual Review of Clinical Psychology. Proposes prenatal maternal distress as a third route (beyond genes and parenting) by which risk gets passed down. Good overview of the HPA, immune, placental, and fetal brain mechanisms involved. Savoca, P.W., Glynn, L.M., Fox, M.M., Richards, M.C. & Callaghan, B.L. (2024). Interoception in pregnancy: Implications for peripartum depression. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. Paul’s paper. A framework paper connecting interoception to peripartum depression risk. Read it after you’ve gone through the interoception papers. 6. Oral Microbiome Citation Notes Gancz, N.N., Querdasi, F.R., Chu, K.A., Towner, E., Taylor, E. & Callaghan, B.L. (2024). Characteristics of the oral microbiome in youth exposed to caregiving adversity. Brain, Behavior, & Immunity – Health. Naomi’s paper. Adversity-exposed kids have a different oral microbiome, and it’s less ‘reactive’ (i.e., has less of a relationship) to cortisol than in comparison kids. Simpson, C.A., Adler, C., du Plessis, M.R., Landau, E.R., Dashper, S.G., Reynolds, E.C., Schwartz, O.S. & Simmons, J.G. (2020). Oral microbiome composition, but not diversity, is associated with adolescent anxiety and depression symptoms. Physiology & Behavior. Not adversity-focused, but a useful methodological reference for how oral microbiome studies in adolescents tend to be designed.
